newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Bosnian Serb denies role in ethnic cleansing.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb denies role in ethnic cleansing.

text.p: A former Bosnian Serb cafe owner and reserve policeman denied on Monday having taken part in a campaign of murder and torture aimed at driving non-Serbs out of northwestern Bosnia in 1992.
Dusan "Dusko" Tadic, 41, was giving his second day of testimony before the U.N. criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia, having taken the stand briefly on Friday.

He says he was not responsible for murders and torture at the Omarska and Keraterm camps in the summer of 1992 after Serb-backed forces swept through northwestern Bosnia displacing non-Serbs. He asserts he is the victim of mistaken identity and was carried along in the tide of chaos in Bosnia in 1992.

Tadic, dressed in a dark suit and tie, looked relaxed and answered questions fluently through a translator although, since the trial began on May 7, he had followed questions and answers from the 75 prosecution witnesses and 37 defence witnesses without using the translation headphones.

Defending British barrister Steven Kay took Tadic through the events of early 1992 during which Tadic had been forced to evacuate his family from his home town of Kozarac to a squalid basement flat in Banja Luka.

Tadic told of the climate of fear and mutual suspicion in Kozarac as war had loomed. He finally decided to move his family to the relative safety of Banja Luka after an attack on the Serb Orthodox church in Kozarac, dodging roadblocks and avoiding groups of armed men.
"During this period had you taken part in any of the "cleansing" activities as they are called in the area?" Kay asked Tadic, who bluntly answered "no".
Tadic said he was settling his family into the flat in Banja Luka, about 40 km (25 miles) south of Kozarac, at the time he is accused of guiding Serb artillery on to his home town.

The Tadic case, the first trial of a war crimes suspect by an international body since the Nuremburg and Tokyo trials after World War Two, was thrown into disarray on Friday after the prosecution withdrew evidence from an eyewitness.

Dragan Opacic, a former prison camp guard, had said he had seen Tadic commit atrocities at the Trnopolje camp in northwestern Bosnia but his evidence was discredited after a U.N. investigator told the court Opacic had been forced by Bosnian military police to give false evidence.

The trial continued smoothly on Monday, with Tadic continuing to face charges of committing war crimes at Omarska and Keraterm. Tadic faces a maximum life jail term if found guilty on 30 other counts of committing atrocities at the camps.

Tadic has never denied visiting Trnopolje and testified on Monday that he had been seen at the camp, armed and in uniform, because he had agreed to go and look for the sister of an elderly acquaintance.

He said he was carrying an automatic rifle given to him by an army deserter and was wearing a pair of thin camouflage overalls over civilian clothes because it was impossible at that time to move around the area without military trappings.

Mobilised into a prized job in the reserve police force in June 1992, Tadic said he had never taken unexplained absences from work because he feared losing his job and being sent to fight on the front lines.
Tribunal sources said the defence was set to wind up its questioning of Tadic by early Tuesday, giving the prosecution its chance to cross-examine him.
There is no time limit on how long the prosecution can take over cross-examination but summing up in the trial is set to begin on November 25 with a verdict expected in the spring.

The tribunal has indicted 75 suspected war criminals. It has seven in its custody, but the rest, including former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and his army commander General Ratko Mladic, remain at liberty.
